One study modeled energy savings from drill-and-fill insulation across different climate zones and found whole-home site energy savings ranging from 8.8% to 13.5% (Polly, et al. 2011). Across the literature, drill-and-fill insulation upgrades are frequently paired with air sealing measures (U.S. Department of Energy 2025) (Brozyna and Badger 2013) (Roberts and Stephenson 2012). More information on air sealing modeling can be found in the advanced air sealing documentation (Phoung, Lou and White 2025). For modeling purposes, drill-and-fill insulation is assumed to be installed properly to a Grade 1 insulation level. According to the RESNET Grading system, Grade 1 assumes installation follows the manufacturer’s instructions and fills the entire wall cavity ( Construction Instruction Experience Center n.d.). However, a field study found that only half of all homes had Grade 1 insulation (North American Insulation Manufacturers Association 2017). In practice, a Grade 1 assumption may be optimistic, and insulation inspection should be conducted carefully (North American Insulation Manufacturers Association 2017). This optimistic assumption about proper insulation installation is a limitation of the work, and may cause modeled results to be different than actual building retrofit results. In summary, this upgrade measure assumes: • Advanced air sealing is applied to dwelling units with ACH50 infiltration rates of 6 or greater. This applies to 92% of all dwelling units and heavily influences the results. • Drill-and-fill insulation is applied to about 30% of dwelling units only • Drill-and-fill insulation uses cellulose up to R-13 on exterior above-grade walls that separate conditioned from unconditioned spaces only • Existing wall cavities with no insulation will receive the insulation, and walls with insulation less than R-13 will not • Proper installation is assumed, similar to Grade 1 RESNET installation. 1.3 Advanced Air Sealing Summary As previously mentioned, drill-and-fill wall insulation is often installed along with air sealing during retrofit projects. Therefore, this drill-and-fill insulation package is modeled with air sealing. Full documentation for the advanced air sealing component of this package is reported separately, but a summary is provided below (Phoung, Lou and White 2025). Air sealing can take various forms, including weatherstripping, caulking, and spray foam. Two common ways to describe air leakage rates are air changes per hour at 50 pascals (ACH50) and cubic feet per minute at 50 pascals (CFM50). ACH50 is used to compare air leakage rates between dwelling units of different sizes, and this metric will be used in this package. 4 This report is available at no cost from the National Laboratory of the Rockies at www.nlr.gov/publications. All dwelling units with an infiltration rate above 6 ACH50 will receive advanced air sealing and then have an infiltration rate of 5 ACH50. This level of advanced air sealing, 5 ACH50, should be considered very aggressive, similar to bringing all residential air leakage down to IECC 2021 new construction levels (3-5 ACH50 depending on climate). In reality, bringing infiltration rates down to this level may require additional enclosure upgrades, such as over cladding of walls, replacing windows, or other techniques that go beyond traditional air sealing practices.
